summary: This document defines usage profiles for DNS over TLS and DTLS, built on one or more authentication mechanisms. They can improve the privacy of DNS lookups compared to plain text. It also specifies new authentication mechanisms.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS queries normally travel in the open, where anyone on the path can read them or answer in place of the real server. This document describes two ways to protect them, and the checks a client can make to be sure it is talking to the server it expects.

subtitle: Two usage profiles, Strict and Opportunistic, and the ways a DNS client can check it is really talking to its encrypted DNS server.

tldr.problem: Cleartext DNS can be watched by passive eavesdroppers and tampered with by active attackers who redirect clients to rogue servers, and encryption alone does not say whether the server is the right one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Strict Privacy profile, where encryption and authentication are required, and an Opportunistic Privacy profile, where they are attempted, plus the ways to authenticate a server with SPKI pin sets or an authentication domain name and a (D)TLS protocol profile for DNS.
tldr.outcome: Clients can choose between the best protection and the best chance of getting an answer, and servers know which credentials and protocol features to offer. The document updates RFC 7858.

today: RFC 8310 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It updates RFC 7858, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DNS Privacy Needs More Than Encryption
sections.content:
DNS privacy issues are discussed in RFC 7626. The two issues most relevant here are passive attacks that eavesdrop on cleartext DNS transactions on the wire, and active attacks that redirect clients to rogue servers to monitor DNS traffic.

Mitigating these attacks increases the privacy of DNS transactions, although many of the other issues raised in RFC 7626 still apply. Two documents already provide ways to increase DNS privacy between DNS clients and DNS servers: DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) and DNS over DTLS (RFC 8094), the latter being an Experimental specification. Both are limited in scope to communication between stub clients and recursive resolvers, and the same scope applies to this document.

Encrypting the query and the response is one way to stop a passive attacker reading them, and it usually brings integrity protection as a side effect, so an on-path attacker cannot simply inject a bogus DNS response. To also stop an active attacker pretending to be the server, the client has to authenticate the (D)TLS connection to the server.

The document also defines a (D)TLS protocol profile for DNS, covering the configuration options and protocol extensions needed by both parties to optimize connection establishment and session resumption, and to support all the authentication mechanisms it specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS queries normally travel in the open, where anyone on the path can read them or answer in place of the real server. This document describes two ways to protect them, and the checks a client can make to be sure it is talking to the server it expects.

sections.title: The Terms the Document Introduces
sections.content:
Several terms are used in a specific way. A DNS client is a DNS stub resolver or forwarder, and for a forwarder the term refers to the side that sends queries. A DNS server is a DNS recursive resolver or forwarder, and for a forwarder it refers to the side that responds to queries; the term does not apply to authoritative servers. A privacy-enabling DNS server implements DNS over TLS, may implement DNS over DTLS, should offer at least one of the credentials the document describes, and implements the (D)TLS profile.

An authentication domain name is a domain name that can be used to authenticate a privacy-enabling DNS server. SPKI pin sets are collections of cryptographic digests that pin public key information, as described in RFC 7858, and constrain a DNS server. Authentication information is what a client may use as the basis of an authentication mechanism: either an SPKI pin set or an authentication domain name.

A reference identifier is one constructed by the DNS client when performing TLS authentication, as described in RFC 6125. A credential is information a server has that proves its identity: a PKIX certificate or a DNSSEC-validated chain to a TLSA record, and it may also include SPKI pin sets.
sections.plainLanguage: The document needs a name for the domain a client uses to check the server. That name is the authentication domain name, and it is the thing the server has to prove.

sections.title: The Two Usage Profiles
sections.content:
A DNS client has a choice of usage profiles. The Strict Privacy profile requires both an encrypted and an authenticated connection to a privacy-enabling DNS server, and a hard failure occurs if this is not available. It mitigates both passive and active attacks, and therefore gives the client the best available privacy for DNS, at the cost of no DNS service if an encrypted, authenticated connection cannot be had.

The Opportunistic Privacy profile uses Opportunistic Security as described in RFC 7435, where cleartext is the baseline and encryption and authentication are applied when available. It may result in an encrypted and authenticated connection, an encrypted connection, or a cleartext connection, depending on the fallback logic of the client, the available authentication information and the capabilities of the DNS server. In all cases the client is willing to continue and resolve queries. Its purpose is to support incremental deployment of increased privacy with a view to widespread adoption of the Strict Privacy profile.

Both profiles can include an initial meta-query performed using Opportunistic Privacy, to obtain the IP address of the privacy-enabling server the client then connects to. Allowing this in the Strict profile avoids significant deployment obstacles, but it means an active attack on the meta-query is possible. Such an attack could cause a Strict Privacy client to connect to a server it cannot authenticate and so get no DNS service, or an Opportunistic Privacy client to connect to a server the attacker controls. DNSSEC validation can detect the attack, which may result in the client not obtaining DNS service at all, depending on its validation policy.

A DNS client SHOULD select a particular usage profile when resolving a query, and MUST NOT fall back from Strict Privacy to Opportunistic Privacy during the resolution of a given query, since that could invalidate the protection against attackers. The Strict Privacy profile provides the best attack mitigation and SHOULD always be implemented in clients that implement the Opportunistic Privacy profile. A client that implements DNS over (D)TLS SHOULD NOT be configured by default to use only cleartext.
sections.plainLanguage: The strict profile refuses to send a query unless the connection is both encrypted and proven. The opportunistic profile sends the query anyway, with whatever protection it can get. That gives a choice between better privacy and always getting an answer.

sections.title: Authentication Mechanisms and How to Combine Them
sections.content:
The document summarises six mechanisms for authenticating a DNS server, and whether the information each needs is configured statically or obtained dynamically. The SPKI mechanism uses an SPKI pin set and an IP address obtained out of band; it leaks the least, but needs ongoing key management. ADN uses an authentication domain name and an IP address obtained out of band, so it needs only a one-off direct configuration. ADN only configures just the domain name and obtains the IP address from A/AAAA meta-queries to a network-provided resolver, which leaks those queries to a server that may be under active attack, an attack that DNSSEC validation can mitigate. DHCP discovers both the domain name and the IP address dynamically, but needs a non-standard or future DHCP option and a secure and trustworthy connection to the DHCP server when used with the Strict profile.

DANE obtains a DNSSEC chain from a DNSSEC-validated lookup, so the client needs a DNSSEC-validating stub implementation, and the chain meta-queries leak to a network-provided server that may be under active attack. The TLS extension takes the DNSSEC chain from the privacy-enabling server itself, in the TLS DNSSEC chain extension, which reduces latency compared with DANE and needs no network-provided DNS server when the domain name and IP address are configured statically; it still needs a DNSSEC-validating stub.

The document gives no recommendation on how an operator should combine an SPKI pin set with a domain-based mechanism. A client configured with both SHOULD match on both a valid credential for the authentication domain name and a valid SPKI pin set, when both are available, and the overall authentication result SHOULD only be considered successful if both mechanisms succeed. It also notes that the authentication domain name is always leaked in the Server Name Indication field of the ClientHello in TLS when communicating with a privacy-enabling DNS server.
sections.plainLanguage: There are six ways to check the server. The client has to know something about the server in advance, or get it from somewhere trustworthy, and then match what the server presents against it. If the client has two kinds of information, it should insist that both match.

sections.title: Where the Authentication Domain Name Comes From
sections.content:
Many (D)TLS clients use PKIX authentication based on an authentication domain name for the server they contact, and they typically look up the server's network address in the DNS before making the connection. Such a client has a bootstrap problem, because it typically only knows the IP address of its DNS server. Before connecting, it has to learn the authentication domain name to associate with that IP address.

The document describes three sources. Full direct configuration means the client is directly and securely provisioned with the authentication domain name of each privacy-enabling DNS server, for example through a client-specific configuration file or API, together with the IP address, both obtained out of band.

Direct configuration of the domain name only means the client is configured directly and securely with only the authentication domain name. The client may learn of a default recursive resolver from an untrusted source, such as the DHCP DNS Recursive Name Server option (RFC 3646), and can then use meta-queries performed with the Opportunistic Privacy profile to an untrusted recursive resolver to establish the IP address of the intended privacy-enabling resolver by looking up A/AAAA records. A DNSSEC-validating client SHOULD apply the same validation policy to those meta-queries as to its other queries, and a client that does not validate DNSSEC SHOULD apply the same policy, if any, to them as well. The client may then cache the server host IP addresses locally so that it need not repeat the meta-query.

Dynamic discovery of both the domain name and the IP address was not possible by any standard means at the time of writing, though a future DHCP extension could provide it. When the Strict Privacy profile is used, the dynamic discovery technique MUST be considered secure and trustworthy; this requirement does not apply to the Opportunistic Privacy profile. A typical DHCP server provides a list of IP addresses for DNS resolvers but no authentication domain name, which prevents the use of most of the ADN-based mechanisms, and this document neither specifies nor requests a DHCP extension to provide one.
sections.plainLanguage: The client usually starts with only an IP address, so it has to learn the name to check the server against. It can be told the name directly, told just the name and looked up the address, or get both from the network, which today needs an option that does not exist.

sections.title: Checking the Server's Credential
sections.content:
When a DNS client configured with an authentication domain name connects to its configured DNS server over (D)TLS, the server may present it with a PKIX certificate. To ensure proper authentication, the DNS client MUST verify the entire certification path per RFC 5280, and additionally use the validation techniques of RFC 6125 to compare the domain name to the certificate provided.

The client constructs one reference identifier for the server based on the authentication domain name: a DNS-ID, which is simply the authentication domain name itself. If that reference identifier is found in the PKIX certificate's subjectAltName extension, as described in Section 6 of RFC 6125, the client should accept the certificate for the server. A compliant DNS client MUST only inspect the certificate's subjectAltName extension for the reference identifier, and in particular MUST NOT inspect the Subject field itself.

DANE (RFC 6698) provides mechanisms that use DNSSEC to anchor trust for certificates and raw public keys, but this requires the client to have an authentication domain name obtained from a trusted source. The specific DANE record for a DNS privacy server takes the form of _853._tcp.[authentication-domain-name] for TLS and _853._udp.[authentication-domain-name] for DTLS.

The client MAY perform the DNS meta-queries for those DANE records itself, using the Opportunistic Privacy profile or in the clear to avoid trust recursion, and the records MUST be validated using DNSSEC. The client MAY also offer the TLS DNSSEC chain extension, in which case the server can provide the full chain in the handshake. If the client offers that extension, it MUST be capable of validating the full DNSSEC authentication chain down to the leaf, and if the supplied chain does not validate, the client MUST ignore it and validate only via other supplied credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: With a normal certificate, the client checks the chain of trust and then looks for the server's domain name in the certificate's alternative name field. With DANE, the client looks up a TLSA record protected by DNSSEC and matches the certificate or key against it.

sections.title: The (D)TLS Protocol Profile
sections.content:
Clients and servers MUST adhere to the (D)TLS implementation recommendations and security considerations of RFC 7525, except with respect to the (D)TLS version. Since encryption of DNS using (D)TLS is a greenfield deployment, DNS clients and servers MUST implement only (D)TLS 1.2 or later; implementing (D)TLS 1.3 is also an option. Implementations MUST NOT offer or provide TLS compression, since compression can leak significant amounts of information, especially to a network observer able to force the user to do an arbitrary DNS lookup, as in CRIME-style attacks.

Implementations compliant with the profile MUST implement TLS session resumption without server-side state (RFC 5077), which eliminates the need for the server to retain cryptographic state for longer than necessary. This statement updates RFC 7858. They MUST also implement raw public keys (RFC 7250), which reduce the size of the ServerHello and can be used by servers that cannot obtain certificates, such as DNS servers on private networks; a client MUST only indicate support for raw public keys if it has an SPKI pin set pre-configured, for interoperability reasons.

Implementations compliant with the profile SHOULD implement TLS False Start (RFC 7918), which reduces round trips by allowing the second flight of messages to also carry the encrypted DNS query, and the Cached Information Extension (RFC 7924), which avoids transmitting the server's certificate and certificate chain if the client has cached that information from a previous handshake.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile sets the rules for the encrypted connection itself: which version of TLS to use, which features to turn on, and which to leave off. Compression is banned because it can leak what was sent.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Traffic Analysis
sections.content:
The security considerations discussed in RFC 7525, RFC 8094, and RFC 7858 apply. DNS clients SHOULD implement support for the mechanisms in Section 8.2, and SHOULD offer a configuration option that limits authentication to those mechanisms, with no fallback to pure PKIX-based authentication, so that authenticating solely through the PKIX infrastructure can be avoided.

Encryption does not stop an attacker from learning things by looking at the traffic. The document suggests measures that reduce the ability of attackers to infer information about encrypted client queries by other means, such as analysis of encrypted traffic size or monitoring of the unencrypted traffic from a recursive resolver to an authoritative server. Clients and servers SHOULD implement EDNS(0) padding (RFC 7830), which allows encrypted queries and responses to hide their size and makes analysis of encrypted traffic harder. Clients SHOULD implement the privacy election of RFC 7871: if a client does not include an edns-client-subnet option with SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH set to 0 in a query, the DNS server may potentially leak client address information to upstream authoritative servers, so the client ought to be able to tell the resolver that it does not want any address information leaked, and the resolver should honour that request.

Appendix A adds a non-normative note on server capability probing. Deployment of DNS over TLS and DTLS will be gradual, not all servers will support either protocol, and the well-known port may be blocked by some middleboxes, so clients are expected to keep track of which servers support which protocol and which have already authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Even with encryption, the size and timing of traffic can give things away. Padding the queries helps hide that. The document also asks clients to be able to say that they do not want their address passed upstream.

items.title: SPKI
items.text: Pin set and IP address obtained out of band; minimal leakage, but ongoing key management is required.

items.title: ADN
items.text: Authentication domain name and IP address obtained out of band; one-off direct configuration.

items.title: ADN only
items.text: Only the domain name is configured; the address comes from meta-queries that can be attacked.

items.title: DHCP
items.text: Both are discovered dynamically, which needs a DHCP option that does not exist yet.

items.title: DANE
items.text: The TLSA record comes from a DNSSEC-validated lookup; needs a DNSSEC-validating stub.

items.title: TLS extension
items.text: The DNSSEC chain arrives in the TLS handshake, which lowers latency but still needs a DNSSEC-validating stub.

items.title: Version 1.2 or later
items.text: Only (D)TLS 1.2 or later may be implemented, since DNS encryption is a greenfield deployment.

items.title: No compression
items.text: Compression must not be offered, because it can leak information in CRIME-style attacks.

items.title: Stateless resumption
items.text: Session resumption without server-side state, so the server need not keep cryptographic state.

items.title: Raw public keys
items.text: Raw public keys shrink the ServerHello and let servers without certificates work.

items.title: False Start
items.text: Recommended, so the DNS query can travel in the second flight of messages.

items.title: Cached information
items.text: Recommended, so the certificate chain need not be sent again.
